opus-5.5.text:
I think the center of gravity is shifting from "can you write the code" to "do you know what's worth building, and can you tell whether it actually works."

When models can generate a thousand lines in a minute, typing speed and syntax memory matter much less. What matters more is, first, **taste and problem definition**. Can you take a vague goal and turn it into something precise enough that a model, or a team, can execute on it? A lot of engineering was always this: deciding what the abstraction should be, which tradeoffs you accept, what you deliberately don't build. AI makes that part more visible, because the execution part gets cheap.

Second, **evaluation and verification**. If you can't judge whether the output is right, a capable model is almost dangerous. It gives you something that looks plausible. Good programmers will be the ones who can design tests, read code critically, notice when something is subtly off, and build the feedback loops that catch mistakes. In research we say the bottleneck often isn't generating ideas, it's having a good eval. I think software is heading the same way.

Third, **understanding systems end to end**. When code is cheap, the hard bugs live in the interactions: the data, the infrastructure, the users, the incentives. People who have a mental model of the whole system, not just their file, become much more valuable.

And maybe the last one is **knowing how to work with the model itself**: knowing what it's good at and where it fails, how to decompose a task so it succeeds, when to trust it and when to take over. It's a bit like managing a very fast, very knowledgeable but sometimes overconfident collaborator. That's a real skill, and I don't think many people have fully developed it yet.

So in a way, the job moves up a level. Less about being the hands, more about being the judgment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding a whole system and its interactions, but does not identify how one’s own work fits into a larger organization.

r002.rationale: It mentions decomposing a task so a model succeeds, but not delegating parts of a complex undertaking to different AIs.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that an ability AI lacks now may cease to be a human advantage six months later.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the thing we used to call "programming ability" is splitting into two parts, and only one of them is going away.

The part that's going away is translation. Turning a clear idea into syntax, remembering APIs, writing the boilerplate, debugging the off-by-one. That was most of what we were graded on, and it's exactly what the models are good at now. If your value as a programmer was that you could write code faster than the person next to you, that advantage is shrinking every few months.

The part that's getting more valuable is everything around that translation step. Three things specifically.

First, knowing what to build and being able to say it precisely. This sounds trivial but it isn't. When I worked on ReAct and later on agents, the hard part was never the implementation. It was figuring out what the right abstraction was, what the environment should look like, what "done" meant. A model can write you a thousand lines in a minute, but it can't tell you whether you asked the right question. Taste in problem selection is now the bottleneck, and taste is hard to automate because it comes from having been wrong a lot.

Second, verification. If you can generate code cheaply, the scarce skill becomes judging whether it's correct, and more importantly, designing the setup so that you can tell. This is why I keep saying the future is about environments and evaluation, not just models. A good programmer in this era thinks like a scientist: what's my hypothesis, what experiment would falsify it, how do I make feedback fast and cheap. People who can build good test harnesses and good reward signals will be worth a lot more than people who can write clever functions.

Third, systems thinking. Models are very good locally and still fairly weak globally. They can write a module, but they're bad at holding the whole architecture in their head over weeks, understanding why a decision made in March constrains what you can do in August. Being able to decompose a large messy thing into pieces an agent can handle, and then integrate the pieces back, is a real skill and it's going to stay human for a while.

There's also a softer thing I'd add. The best programmers I know are the ones who are comfortable not knowing. They can sit in a half-understood problem without panicking and just keep poking at it. With AI, the people who struggle are often the ones who want the tool to give them certainty. The people who thrive treat the model as a very fast, slightly unreliable collaborator and keep their own judgment in the loop.

So if a student asked me what to practice, I would not say "learn more languages." I'd say: do projects where you have to decide what to build, get really good at writing evaluations, and read a lot of other people's systems to understand why they're shaped the way they are. The coding itself, you'll pick up as you go, and increasingly the model will do most of it anyway.

r002.rationale: It describes breaking a large undertaking into pieces an agent can handle, but does not mention delegating tasks to different AIs.

astra-6.text:
I think the emphasis will shift from writing code to deciding what code should be written, and understanding whether it actually solves the problem. If you have a very clear specification, AI can do more and more of the implementation. But in practice, the specification is often the hard part. What does the user need? What constraints matter? What are you willing to trade off?

So one important ability is turning an ambiguous problem into something concrete. Another is judgment: when the AI gives you a solution, can you evaluate it? Can you recognize that it passes the tests but rests on the wrong assumption, or that it works now but will be difficult to maintain? Technical understanding still matters because you need to know where to look and what questions to ask.

I also think good programmers will become better at experimenting. When implementation becomes cheaper, you can try several approaches instead of spending all your time on the first one. The advantage goes to people who can learn from those experiments and choose a useful direction. Writing code remains part of the work, but taking responsibility for the whole outcome becomes more important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ability to define problems will become more important than the ability to implement a clearly specified solution. If you know exactly what you want, AI can increasingly help you write the code. But deciding what is worth building, understanding the constraints, and figuring out whether the result actually solves the problem—that still requires judgment.

So a good programmer needs to move between levels of abstraction. You should be able to discuss the user’s goal, think through the system design, and then go into the details when something fails. If you only look at the high-level description, you might miss a subtle bug. If you only focus on the code, you might solve the wrong problem very efficiently.

And I think verification becomes more valuable. As generating code gets cheaper, the bottleneck shifts toward knowing which code to trust. Can you design a meaningful test? Can you recognize a flawed assumption? Can you give the AI useful feedback? Those abilities depend on technical understanding, so I don’t think learning the fundamentals becomes unnecessary. They give you the judgment to use these tools well.
